Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
OK. Here's a parallel example so that hopefully people can begin to
view this thing objectively:

Anne plays 10,000 games of foo in the red region.
Barbara plays 10,000 games of foo in the green region.

Anne's record is 10,000 wins and no losses.
Barbara's record is no wins and 10,000 losses.

Now, from this data alone, does it follow that Anne is a better
player than Barbara? No.

For instance, pehaps the game of foo is chess and the green region
is composed of exactly two players, Barbara aka Bobby Fischer and
Deep Blue, while the red region is composed of exactly two players,
Anne aka Roger Fox and a hamster.

That is *not* to say that the above is the case. Only that the
"proof" is flawed. It could very well be that the conclusion
(Anne is better than Barbara) is true - what is disputed it that
the conclusion follows inescapably from the evidence. It does not.

If, however, it is reasonable to *assume* that the overall quality of
players is statistically the same (by whatever measure is appropriate)
in the two regions, /then/ it is reasonable to *assume* that Anne is
a better player than Barbara. (Still not proven, of course).

That, I think, pretty much covers the meaningful parts of both sides
of the debate.

--
L. Scott Johnson (sjoh...@math.sc.edu)
http://www.math.sc.edu/~sjohnson

It's a good reduction of part of the argument. Another part of it is
just Legbiter and I butting heads on logical proofs, understanding
of proper statistical treatment of a subjects, and so forth.

I do sense a true difference of opinion about whether different events
at different places can actually vary significantly in terms of quality
of competition. Legbiter doesn't seem to believe that can be but if he'd
experienced what I've experienced as I've played in various places, I
strongly believe he wouldn't doubt it. Whether those experiences are
applicable to comparisons of top players - for instance, explaining Rob
Treasure's record in England in comparison to Ben Peal's in the U.S. is
clearly indeterminate. I guess I just sort of resent people waving their
hand over that lack of data and somehow managing to conclude that, "We
have no way of knowing so I must be right." Lovely.

Fred

Just to toss another wrench into the works--

Whenever professionals do random statistical sampling, the magic
number is 51 to allow them to consider the results "statistically
significant." I'm not quite sure if this applies (or has even already
been discussed at length), but I would venture you can't even MAKE a
statement comparing two "independent" groups of players unless the
sample size is 51 or greater. :)

Messages.Author: The Horror
Messages.Body:

> Whenever professionals do random statistical sampling, the magic
> number is 51 to allow them to consider the results "statistically
> significant." I'm not quite sure if this applies (or has even already
> been discussed at length), but I would venture you can't even MAKE a
> statement comparing two "independent" groups of players unless the
> sample size is 51 or greater. :)

WTF? Firstly, the less the number of people in a sample group, the more you
have to use statistics to compare the results. There is no magic number for
doing statistics. You do statistics with what you have. If your sample
group is large enough, you don't even have to use statistics because the
sample mean approaches the group mean, and statistical errors decrease with
increasing sample size.

Secondly, I don't know what you are saying about 51 being the magic number
for significance. When performing significance tests it is common to use
95% as the significance level, often even more like 99% or 99.99%.

I'm not going to launch into an explanation of what this actually means in
real terms. It just occured to me that it would require way too much effort
to do so, and that anyone who knows anything about statistics would be bored
silly by it anyhow.

Thalles

Surely you jest. If gather information on a pool of 10 people
representing a certain population, then gather information on 100
people representing an independent yet similarly sized population, you
know a lot more about the group from which you sampled 100.

> If your sample
> group is large enough, you don't even have to use statistics because the
> sample mean approaches the group mean, and statistical errors decrease with
> increasing sample size.

Yes, and your sample group should be 51 to be considered "large
enough." Anything beyond that number adds relatively little
significant information since you've surpassed the 95% threshhold.

> Secondly, I don't know what you are saying about 51 being the magic number
> for significance. When performing significance tests it is common to use
> 95% as the significance level, often even more like 99% or 99.99%.

Exactly. Having a random sample of 51 from a given population gives
you the 95% significance level so you can be confident in your
numbers.

Can't be that simple. Sweden has a grand total of nine million. The
westcoastregion where I play has some two million inhabitants.
Gothenburg numbers 450 000. In Gothenburg we're 34 registered players
and play casually twice a week gathering aprox ten players both days out
of an active group of 15. Monthly tournaments have gone back to ten
players, but we'll find a way to up that number.
Spring EC-qualifier at Gothcon attracted 35 players.

I don't know about the rest of Europe, but Sweden has a tradition of
non-profit work. Gothcon (yearly gaming convention in Gothenburg) totals
around 1100 unique individuals - no salaries involved at all.

If people expect to put in unpaid work - and still get the response as
if paid, ie get shouted at sometimes, I believe it's easier to create
an active group doing whatever. Especially as the only thing
unforgivable is inactivity - punishment is meeted out by means of
